question: Does idealism explain experience or merely make it primitive?
why_it_matters: This is the most common objection to idealism from physicalists and neutral monists alike. If idealism simply posits consciousness as fundamental without explaining why experience has the structure it does, it offers no advantage over physicalism. The question determines whether idealism is a genuine explanatory framework or a nominal redefinition.

candidate_explanations.name: Idealism as genuinely explanatory
candidate_explanations.best_case: Idealism explains the structure of experience through the self-articulation of consciousness. Manifestation has a logical structure (icchā-jñāna-kriyā) that explains why experience takes the forms it does. Consciousness is not a brute primitive but a self-differentiating reality whose intrinsic dynamics generate the phenomenal world.
hard_to_vary_core: The inherent structure of consciousness (prakāśa-vimarśa) explains why experience is manifest rather than dark.
The icchā-jñāna-kriyā triad explains the structural features of experience: desire to know generates intentional directedness.
Idealism explains the unity of experience: all contents are modifications of a single field, which physicalism must treat as a mystery.
current_problems: The explanatory content of idealism must be distinguished from mere redescription: does icchā-jñāna-kriyā explain anything that physicalism cannot?
Idealism must account for the specific regularities of nature (physical laws) without treating them as arbitrary or epiphenomenal.
The account must explain why consciousness appears to be generated by brains, even if the appearance is ultimately deceptive.

falsifiers.condition: A demonstration that every explanatory claim of idealism can be translated without loss into physicalist or neutral monist terms, showing idealism adds no content.
A complete neuroscientific explanation of phenomenal structure (binding, qualia differentiation, unity) that requires no conscious substrate.

candidate_explanations.name: Idealism as primitive posit
candidate_explanations.best_case: Idealism simply names consciousness as fundamental without explaining why it has the structure it does. It provides no mechanism for the differentiation of experiences, their correlation with brain states, or their lawful behaviour. Making consciousness primitive is not an explanation but a refusal to explain.
hard_to_vary_core: Positing consciousness as fundamental is methodologically identical to positing matter as fundamental: both are brutely given.
Idealism offers no account of why consciousness differentiates into the specific contents we observe rather than any others.
The correlation between experience and brain states is left unexplained: if consciousness is fundamental, why does it track brain function?
current_problems: The objection equally applies to physicalism: making matter primitive is no more explanatory than making consciousness primitive.
Idealism can appeal to structural principles (icchā-jñāna-kriyā, kañcukas) that physicalism lacks for explaining phenomenal structure.
Physicalism has no explanation for why matter is accompanied by experience; idealism has no explanation for why experience has lawful structure—the explanatory burden is symmetric.

falsifiers.condition: A demonstration that physicalism provides a positive explanation for the presence of experience that does not reduce to brute correlation or elimination.

candidate_explanations.name: Dual-aspect identity as alternative
candidate_explanations.best_case: Both idealism and physicalism make unwarranted primitives. The better framework is dual-aspect monism: consciousness and matter are two aspects of a deeper reality. This dissolves the explanatory demand on both sides and accounts for correlation without reducing either term.
hard_to_vary_core: The intrinsic nature of matter may be phenomenal, as Russell argued; physical descriptions capture only structural/dispositional properties.
Dual-aspect monism explains why consciousness and brain activity correlate without making either ontologically dependent on the other.
It avoids the primitive-positing objection by locating explanation at a deeper level.
current_problems: Dual-aspect monism may simply postpone the primitive to a third term that is equally mysterious.
It must explain how the two aspects relate to the neutral substrate without introducing a third aspect or reintroducing duality.
The view is structurally similar to Trika but lacks the internal differentiation (icchā-jñāna-kriyā) that generates manifold experience.

falsifiers.condition: A proof that any dual-aspect theory collapses into either idealism or physicalism under analysis of the relation between aspect and substrate.

cruxes.question: Does physicalism face a symmetric explanatory burden to idealism regarding the primitive posit?

candidate_pressure.cand:idealism-primitive-posit: no, physicalism explains structure, idealism does not

cruxes.question: Does the icchā-jñāna-kriyā triad provide genuine explanatory content or is it a redescription?
Which framework better explains the brain-consciousness correlation?

candidate_pressure.cand:dual-aspect-anchoring: correlation is necessary given dual-aspect identity

initial_state_of_play.current_best_answer: The objection that idealism merely makes consciousness primitive is serious but symmetric with physicalism. The icchā-jñāna-kriyā framework offers a structural explanation that goes beyond brute posit, but its explanatory content must be demonstrated through specific predictions and formal models rather than asserted. Dual-aspect monism provides an alternative but may not escape the same objection.
initial_state_of_play.confidence_language: symmetric explanatory burdens, Trika offers structural resources
next_tests: Formalise the icchā-jñāna-kriyā triad as a generative framework for phenomenal structure and test whether it predicts features physicalism cannot.
Develop a rigorous comparison of explanatory power (using e.g. predictive scope, parsimony, coherence) between idealism and physicalism on the same phenomena.
Produce a Russellian monism version that incorporates Trika's internal differentiation to see if it outperforms both pure idealism and pure physicalism.
implications: If idealism is genuinely explanatory, the research programme shifts from defending against the primitive-positing objection to generating testable predictions about phenomenal structure.
If idealism is merely a primitive posit, the consciousness-first programme must accept that it is a metaphysical stance grounded in phenomenology rather than a superior explanation.
If dual-aspect monism with Trika internal differentiation succeeds, it offers a synthesis that may dissolve the hard problem as traditionally framed.
